name: French Green
lede: French green is a muted, slightly yellowish green that the dictionaries file under a country adjective, and that the paint trade used for an altogether different thing.

sections.title: Two uses of the name
sections.body:
Paterson's dictionary lists French green among a run of colors prefixed with French, and describes it as a yellowy green [1]. The pigment trade used the name differently: the Pigment Compendium records it as one of the less common names for [[emerald-green]], citing Fiedler and Bayard [2]. Emerald green is a harsher, bluer and far more poisonous color than this swatch, so the two should not be confused.

The books say nothing further about where the name came from, and who first called a green French is undocumented in our sources [1][2].

sections.title: The swatch
sections.body:
The color on this page comes from the systematic charts, not from a pigment. It carries over from Ridgway's 1886 *Nomenclature of Colors*, reappears in his 1912 *Color Standards*, and sits in ISCC-NBS block 136, where the 1955 dictionary calls it a moderate yellowish green, 5.3 units away [3]. Maerz and Paul's dictionary gives dates of 1618 for one nearby plate and about 1794 for another, which hints at an old name but pins nothing down [3].

Its nearest named neighbors are [[slate-green]] and [[viridian]], 6.4 units from the latter, and the library lists Zinc Green as a near-duplicate, 1.0 apart [3]. Next to [[green]] in a swatch row it reads as a grey-leaning, slightly warm leaf green.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
This is a rare color in paint. It appears in 66 of 23,781 paintings in our archive (0.28 per cent), and in 20 when counted by the stricter within-painting lens [4]. It is rarer than 61 per cent of named colors, and when it does appear it is most often a mid-tone, in 55 per cent of those 20 [4].

It peaks in the 1900s, found in 8 of 1,674 paintings from those years, about four times the rate the same museums would predict [4]. The earliest match is a work of 1480, but that is a look-alike hue 406 years older than the name's earliest record in our sources, 1886 [4]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a color match is a look-alike hue and not a pigment test. [4]

origin.source: Paterson, A Dictionary of Colour, p. 177; Pigment Compendium, p. 174

disambiguation.gloss: the pigment trade sometimes used French green as another name for it; the swatch here is far duller

questions.q: In the pigment trade, French green was sometimes another name for which paint?
True or false: the swatch on this page was taken from a pigment.

openers: French green was sometimes just another name for emerald green in the paint trade, a far harsher color than the swatch.
Look for it as a mid-tone: when it appears in a painting it is usually the color in the middle of the range.
